title: Brewers Pick Up William Contreras Option, Decline Senzatela and Sánchez Deals – MLB Trade Rumors
body:
Milwaukee’s front office moved swiftly this week, confirming that catcher William Contreras will remain under contract for another season while opting out of two sizeable options on the mound. The Brewers exercised the $14.5 million club option on Contreras, extending his stay through 2025, and simultaneously declined a $14 million option on reliever Antonio Senzatela as well as the team’s portion of an $8.5 million mutual option on right‑hander Luis Sánchez. The decisions, largely expected for the catcher and the two pitchers, reshape the club’s payroll and signal how Milwaukee plans to balance its roster ahead of a competitive 2024 campaign.

Contreras, who posted a career‑high .282 batting average with 19 home runs and 71 RBIs in 2023, has become a cornerstone of Milwaukee’s offense and a steady presence behind the plate. By exercising the option, the Brewers lock in a player who not only contributes at the plate but also handles a pitching staff that has been among the league’s best in strikeouts. The move eliminates any offseason speculation about his free‑agency status and gives the team a clear starting point for its 2025 budget. It also underscores the organization’s belief that Contreras can continue to develop his power and defensive framing, attributes that were instrumental in the Brewers’ push to the postseason last year.

The decision to pass on Senzatela’s $14 million option was less surprising. The 30‑year‑old right‑hander posted a 4.34 ERA over 71 innings in 2023, a regression from his 2022 breakout season when he posted a sub‑3.00 ERA and earned All‑Star honors. While his fastball still sits in the mid‑90s, diminished command and an uptick in walks have raised concerns about his long‑term value at a premium price. By declining the option, Milwaukee preserves flexibility to explore lower‑cost alternatives in free agency or the trade market, and it can potentially re‑sign Senzatela on a shorter, more team‑friendly deal if his performance rebounds.

The mutual option involving Luis Sánchez presented a more nuanced calculus. The veteran right‑hander, who has been a reliable back‑of‑the‑rotation arm for Milwaukee, posted a 3.84 ERA across 108 innings last season, striking out 115 batters. However, his contract includes a clause that would have required the club to pay $8.5 million for a guaranteed 2025 season, a figure that exceeds his projected market value given recent trends for middle‑relief pitchers. By walking away from the club side of the option, the Brewers avoid a costly commitment while retaining the right to negotiate a new contract should both parties find terms agreeable. This approach mirrors a broader league pattern where teams prefer short‑term, performance‑based deals for bullpen pieces rather than long‑term guarantees.

Financially, the combined effect of these moves trims roughly $22 million from the Brewers’ 2025 payroll, offsetting the $14.5 million outlay on Contreras. The savings afford Milwaukee additional latitude to address other needs, such as bolstering the outfield depth or adding a left‑handed reliever—areas that have been identified as weak spots during the 2023 season. The front office’s willingness to part with high‑priced options also suggests confidence that the core of the roster—particularly the starting rotation anchored by Corbin Burnes and Brandon Woodruff—remains competitive without heavy spending on the bullpen.

Looking ahead, the Brewers now enter the offseason with a clearer picture of their financial ceiling and a defined set of priorities. Retaining Contreras locks in a key piece of the lineup, while the flexibility gained from the declined options positions Milwaukee to be an active participant in the upcoming free‑agency market. Whether the club will pursue a high‑impact reliever, add depth to its bench, or explore trades for emerging talent remains to be seen, but the recent roster moves indicate a strategic intent to blend stability with fiscal prudence. As spring training approaches, Milwaukee’s decisions this week will serve as a blueprint for how the Brewers aim to contend in an increasingly competitive National League Central.
